lesson.title: Collections, comprehensions and f-strings
lesson.note: Lists, dicts and comprehensions cover most day-to-day Python; f-strings handle the formatting.
lesson.code:
# Everything is an object, and names are just labels
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]

squares = [n * n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
total   = sum(nums)

print("numbers :", nums)
print("squares :", squares)
print("total   :", total, " mean:", round(total / len(nums), 2))

lookup = {name: len(name) for name in ["algorithm", "cache", "pointer"]}
for word, length in sorted(lookup.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]):
    print(f"{word:<10} {length} letters")

lesson.title: Reading and writing files
lesson.note: Open, write, read back, then count words — the shape of almost every text-processing script.
lesson.code:
# Write a file, read it back, count the words
text = """the quick brown fox
jumps over the lazy dog
the dog barks"""

with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(text)

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    lines = f.read().splitlines()

counts = {}
for line in lines:
    for word in line.split():
        counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1

print(f"{len(lines)} lines, {sum(counts.values())} words, {len(counts)} unique")
for word, n in sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:5]:
    print(f"  {word:<6} {n}")
lesson.output:
3 lines, 12 words, 9 unique
  the    3
  dog    2
  barks  1
  brown  1
  fox    1

lesson.title: Round-robin scheduling
lesson.note: Each process gets a fixed quantum before being sent to the back of the queue — the basis of time-sharing.
lesson.code:
# Round-robin scheduling with a quantum of 3
jobs = [("P1", 7), ("P2", 4), ("P3", 9), ("P4", 2)]
quantum, clock = 3, 0
remaining = dict(jobs)
queue = [name for name, _ in jobs]
finish = {}

while queue:
    name = queue.pop(0)
    slice_ = min(quantum, remaining[name])
    print(f"t={clock:>2}  run {name} for {slice_}")
    clock += slice_
    remaining[name] -= slice_
    if remaining[name]:
        queue.append(name)
    else:
        finish[name] = clock

print()
total = 0
for name, burst in jobs:
    turnaround = finish[name]
    total += turnaround
    print(f"{name}  burst {burst}  finished at {finish[name]:>2}  turnaround {turnaround}")
print(f"\naverage turnaround: {total/len(jobs):.2f}")

lesson.title: Subnetting a /24
lesson.note: Splitting an address block into smaller subnets, with the usable host range for each.
lesson.code:
import ipaddress

net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.10.0/24")
print(f"network   {net}")
print(f"netmask   {net.netmask}")
print(f"hosts     {net.num_addresses - 2}")

print("split into /26 subnets:")
for sub in net.subnets(new_prefix=26):
    hosts = list(sub.hosts())
    print(f"  {str(sub):<18} {hosts[0]} .. {hosts[-1]}")

lesson.title: Hashing and the avalanche effect
lesson.note: One changed character rewrites roughly half the digest bits — and chaining hashes gives you a blockchain.
lesson.code:
import hashlib

def sha(text):
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()

# One changed character avalanches through the whole digest
a, b = "open computer science", "open computer scienca"
ha, hb = sha(a), sha(b)

print(f"{a!r}\n  {ha}")
print(f"{b!r}\n  {hb}")

diff = sum(x != y for x, y in zip(bin(int(ha,16))[2:].zfill(256), bin(int(hb,16))[2:].zfill(256)))
print(f"\n{diff} of 256 bits differ ({diff/256:.1%})")

# A three-block chain, each block committing to the one before
prev = "0" * 64
for i, payload in enumerate(["alice->bob 5", "bob->carol 2", "carol->dan 1"], 1):
    prev = sha(prev + payload)
    print(f"block {i}  {payload:<14} {prev[:32]}...")

lesson.title: Truth tables and counting
lesson.note: Every propositional connective in one table, then permutations and combinations from factorials.
lesson.code:
from itertools import product

print(" p  q | p^q  pvq  p->q  p<->q")
print("-" * 33)
for p, q in product([True, False], repeat=2):
    implies = (not p) or q
    iff     = p == q
    print(f" {int(p)}  {int(q)} |  {int(p and q)}    {int(p or q)}     {int(implies)}      {int(iff)}")

print()
n = 5
fact = lambda k: 1 if k <= 1 else k * fact(k - 1)
print(f"permutations P(5,3) = {fact(5)//fact(2)}")

lesson.title: Solving systems and finding eigenvalues
lesson.note: NumPy's linear algebra module answers most matrix questions in one line each.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])
b = np.array([8., 13.])

x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)

print("solving Ax = b")
print("  x        =", np.round(x, 4))
print("  check Ax =", np.round(A @ x, 4))
print()
print("eigenvalues  :", np.round(np.sort(vals), 4))
print("determinant  :", round(float(np.linalg.det(A)), 4))
print("condition no :", round(float(np.linalg.cond(A)), 4))

lesson.title: Fitting a line by least squares
lesson.note: The closed-form solution recovers the slope and intercept that generated the data, even through the noise.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 60)
y = 2.4 * x + 1.7 + rng.normal(0, 1.5, x.size)

X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
w = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]

pred = X @ w
r2 = 1 - ((y - pred) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()

print(f"intercept : {w[0]:.3f}   (true 1.700)")
print(f"slope     : {w[1]:.3f}   (true 2.400)")
print(f"R^2       : {r2:.4f}")

lesson.title: Backpropagation from scratch
lesson.note: A 2-4-1 network learns XOR with no framework at all — just matrix multiplies and the chain rule.
lesson.code:
import numpy as np

# A 2-2-1 network learning XOR, written out by hand
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = np.array([[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([[0],[1],[1],[0]], dtype=float)

sig  = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
dsig = lambda a: a * (1 - a)

W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)), np.zeros((1, 4))
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)), np.zeros((1, 1))

for epoch in range(1, 4001):
    h  = sig(X @ W1 + b1)
    out = sig(h @ W2 + b2)
    loss = ((out - y) ** 2).mean()

    d2 = (out - y) * dsig(out)
    d1 = (d2 @ W2.T) * dsig(h)
    W2 -= 0.5 * h.T @ d2;  b2 -= 0.5 * d2.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    W1 -= 0.5 * X.T @ d1;  b1 -= 0.5 * d1.sum(0, keepdims=True)

    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>4}   loss {loss:.6f}")

print()
for xi, p in zip(X, sig(sig(X @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2)):
    print(f"  {int(xi[0])} XOR {int(xi[1])} -> {p[0]:.4f}")
